name: Porcelain veneers
lead: Porcelain veneers are thin, custom-made shells, usually of porcelain or glass-ceramic, bonded to the front of teeth to change their colour, shape, size or spacing.[1][2] They are made indirectly by a dental technician, unlike composite veneers, which can be built directly in the mouth.[1]

A 2016 meta-analysis of clinical trials on feldspathic porcelain and glass-ceramic laminate veneers examined survival and complications including debonding and fracture,[3] and a ten-year prospective trial followed 87 veneers in 25 patients.[4] Wikipedia reports lifespans of 10 to 30 years with modern bonding, with reasons for replacement including chipping, discoloration and decay, and notes that preparation can remove tooth structure.[1]
infobox: Some enamel removal; thin 'no-prep' types exist[1]

paras: Wikipedia credits California dentist Charles Pincus with making veneers for film actors in 1928 and acrylic versions in 1937, Michael Buonocore's enamel-etching work in 1959 as the basis for bonding, and Simonsen and Calamia in 1982-83 with showing porcelain could be etched with hydrofluoric acid for a durable bond.[1] A 1985 review described etched porcelain veneers as a current technique.[5]
Dentists commonly remove some enamel, using window, feather, bevel or incisal-overlap designs, may place temporary veneers, and then bond the final shells.[1]

Wikipedia reports that preparation may remove about 3-30% of the tooth surface depending on technique, that sensitivity and decay can occur, and that critics say veneers are overused for minor issues.[1] A clinician's 15-year review described patterns of veneer failure and stressed informing patients of limitations.[6] Contraindications listed include poor hygiene, gum disease, grinding and little enamel.[1] 'Turkey teeth' and other overseas veneer packages are discussed in other entries.

A literature review of laboratory and clinical work examined factors influencing long-term success.[2] The 2016 meta-analysis evaluated survival and complication rates for feldspathic and glass-ceramic laminates.[3] The prospective trial assessed esthetics, marginal integrity, retention, fracture and patient satisfaction at 5 and 10 years, recalling 93% of restorations at 10 years.[4] Retrospective evaluations covered 6-12 years.[7] Registered trials continue on cementation, colour stability and sectional versus full veneers.[8][9][10]

timeline.event: Charles Pincus makes temporary veneers for film actors.[1]
Buonocore's enamel-etching work begins the path to bonding.[1]
Etching of porcelain with hydrofluoric acid enables durable bonded veneers.[1]

card.summary: Thin ceramic shells bonded to the front of teeth; long-lasting in follow-up studies but they usually require irreversible enamel removal.
card.note: Enamel removal is generally permanent; costs and longevity vary with dentist and case.

quick.overview:
Porcelain veneers are custom ceramic shells bonded to front teeth to change colour, shape or spacing. They are among the best-studied cosmetic dental restorations, with long-term clinical trials and meta-analyses.

Wikipedia gives lifespans of 10 to 30 years, with chipping, debonding, decay and discoloration as reasons for replacement.
quick.mechanism: A dentist usually removes some enamel, takes an impression or scan, and a lab makes the shells, which are etched and bonded to the tooth with resin cement.
quick.risks: Reported risks are sensitivity, decay, debonding and fracture; preparation can remove a meaningful part of the tooth surface, and critics argue veneers are overused. Costs are substantial.
